1	# Planetfall
2	
3	Planetfall is a 3D browser game about a stranded astronaut whose ship AI has
4	lost its memory. To get home, the player restores the ship's memory while
5	learning the real [Entire](https://docs.entire.io) checkpoint workflow — three
6	levels, one arc:
7	
8	1. **First Memories** — bank your own work: commit it, then link the
9	   checkpoint. Freeze keeps it; checkpoint banks it.
10	2. **The Drone Bay** — five subagents repair the ship in parallel while you
11	   can only be in one place. `entire checkpoint explain` shows you what each
12	   one did; `entire dispatch` turns the day into a report.
13	3. **Launch Clearance** — the finale. From the pilot's chair, the ship's AI
14	   asks questions only the record can answer. Pick the tool — a command, or a
15	   skill that runs it for you — confirm the answers, complete the launch code,
16	   and lift off.
17	
18	The thread through all three: work you didn't watch is never a mystery if it
19	was checkpointed. You weren't there — your checkpoints were.
20	
21	## Run
22	
23	```bash
24	npm install
25	npm run dev
26	```
27	
28	Open <http://localhost:5173>.
29	
30	Useful commands:
31	
32	```bash
33	npm run build
34	npm run dev -- --host 127.0.0.1
35	```
36	
37	Development shortcuts:
38	
39	- `?view=island` — straight to Level 1.
40	- `?view=level2` (or `?level=2`) — Level 2 with Level 1 checkpoints preloaded.
41	- `?view=level3` (or `?level=3`) — Level 3, the cockpit finale.
42	- `?view=archive` — a shelved search level kept playable for later.
43	
44	## How To Play
45	
46	Orbit view:
47	
48	- Drag to orbit the planet, scroll to zoom, click the island pin to land.
49	
50	On the island (Levels 1–2):
51	
52	- Click to capture the mouse; move with WASD or the arrow keys.
53	- `M` toggles a bird's-eye map (you can keep walking), `Esc` releases the
54	  mouse or closes finished terminal output, `B` returns to orbit.
55	
56	**Level 1 — First Memories.** Walk to a glowing memory; the ship terminal
57	opens. Type `git add`, then `git commit` to freeze it in ice. When Entire
58	offers to link the commit, press `y` — only linked checkpoints fill the ship
59	memory meter. Bank all three, then run `entire checkpoint list` before the
60	countdown hits `0:00`.
61	
62	**Level 2 — The Drone Bay.** Five systems are dark and the clock can't be
63	beaten alone. Press `E` at a broken system and a subagent takes the job while
64	you move on — running all five at once is the whole point. When a beam turns
65	ice-blue, walk up: `entire checkpoint explain` comes pre-filled; press `Enter`,
66	read what the subagent actually did, then ADD TO SHIP (`Y`). After the fifth
67	accept, type `entire dispatch` to file the day's report.
68	
69	**Level 3 — Launch Clearance.** No walking — you're in the pilot's chair, and
70	the launch computer won't arm on work nobody can account for. The ship asks
71	five questions about work you never watched. Pick a way to look each one up
72	(`1`–`3`): a raw command, a skill that runs it for you, or — occasionally — a
73	dead end that costs only seconds. The answer lands on screen; confirm it to
74	lock a launch-code segment. Five segments, then `entire dispatch` files the
75	flight log: ignition, fireworks, liftoff.
76	
77	Winning a level offers `Enter` to carry you straight into the next. Failing
78	only ever offers `R` to retry — the clock is the only enemy.
79	
80	## Current Features
81	
82	- Procedural lavender ocean planet with metallic gold islands, atmosphere,
83	  clouds, stars, and a Saturn-style ring.
84	- Orbit-to-island flow with a tracked landing pin and crossfade transitions;
85	  wins chain levels directly with `Enter`.
86	- Walkable first-person island terrain, plus a bird's-eye map toggle.
87	- Diegetic terminals that accept the real workflow: `git add`, `git commit`,
88	  checkpoint linking, `entire checkpoint list` / `explain` / `search`, and
89	  `entire dispatch` — pre-filled where typing ids would be friction.
90	- Five worker subagents that improvise upgrades in parallel (a bent dish comes
91	  back as a signal spire), each job sealed under a checkpoint to review.
92	- A cockpit finale: rotating tool menus (commands and skills as different
93	  lenses on the same record), answer confirms, a filling launch code, and a
94	  3-2-1 ignition with fireworks on the climb out.
95	- Ice-block commit metaphor, checkpoint record cards, and in-world
96	  `Entire-Checkpoint: <id>` trailer labels matching the real shape.
97	- One countdown per level with urgent/critical clock states and a panic sky;
98	  fail screens with instant retry.
99	- Local background music with play, mute, and volume controls.
100	
101	## How It's Built
102	
103	- **Three.js + Vite** power the app.
104	- `index.html` defines the canvas, per-level HUD blocks, terminals, briefings,
105	  countdowns, win/fail screens, loader, and audio controls.
106	- `src/main.js` owns the renderer, view switching and level progression,
107	  resizing, and the render loop.
108	- `src/planetView.js` builds the orbit scene: planet, clouds, atmosphere,
109	  ring, stars, controls, and the landable island pin.
110	- `src/islandView.js` is Level 1: terrain, memory artifacts, the terminal
111	  state machine, countdown, checkpoint logic, failure, and reset.
112	- `src/droneBayView.js` is Level 2: five broken systems, five subagents,
113	  pre-filled explain reviews, and the dispatch finish line.
114	- `src/launchView.js` is Level 3: the cockpit rig, question/tool/answer
115	  console, launch code, and the liftoff sequence.
116	- `src/archiveView.js` is the shelved search level, kept playable.
117	- `src/overhead.js` adds the bird's-eye map; `src/firstPerson.js` wraps
118	  `PointerLockControls` for terrain-glued walking.
119	- `src/memoryProps.js` holds the shared beam/ice/checkpoint-id props;
120	  `src/debris.js` defines the memory artifacts.
121	- `src/terrain.js`, `src/planet.js`, `src/noise.js`, `src/atmosphere.js`, and
122	  `src/ring.js` generate the procedural terrain and planet visuals.
123	
124	Most visual assets are generated at runtime; the music is bundled locally in
125	`public/audio/asteroid-circuit.mp3`.
126	
127	## Project History
128	
129	This repo started as `signalkit`, a Python telemetry CLI. On June 5, 2026 it
130	pivoted into Planetfall: a procedural Three.js game for teaching Entire through
131	play. The old code and the design evolution are recoverable through git history
132	and Entire checkpoints.
133	
```

1	# Planetfall — Plan & Status
2	
3	_Last updated: 2026-06-10_
4	
5	## The pitch
6	
7	You're a stranded astronaut. Your ship's AI has **amnesia** — it lost all its
8	context about what happened. To escape, you explore a 3D planet, find debris,
9	and each piece hides a small puzzle solved by **recovering lost context**.
10	
11	The hook: reconstructing the ship's memory in-fiction **is the same act** as
12	recovering a real codebase's history with [Entire](https://docs.entire.io).
13	Each puzzle teaches a real `entire` command.
14	
15	> Note: `entire explain` does **not** exist (it was an early guess). The real
16	> context-recovery commands are `recap`, `checkpoint`, `activity`, `dispatch`.
17	
18	## Locked decisions
19	
20	- **3D, web-based.** Three.js + Vite, no downloaded assets — the planet is
21	  generated procedurally at load.
22	- **Planet look (approved):** a dreamy **lavender ocean world** with a few
23	  **gold metallic islands** that shimmer, wrapped in a **Saturn-style ring**.
24	  Soft, minimal, calm.
25	  - NOT earthlike. NOT the glowing-magenta-"neural"-vein look (tried it; it
26	    looked "itchy" — busy land texture fighting bright veins. Removed.)
27	  - Keep lighting (sun / ambient / env) **low** — the lavender sea washes out
28	    white if over-lit.
29	- **Build order:** get the world feeling right **first** (done), then puzzles,
30	  then the command engine + win/lose.
31	- **Two-level structure (approved 2026-06-05):** the game is two views, not one.
32	  - **Orbit view** — bird's-eye planet; click a marked **island hotspot** to land.
33	  - **Island view** — a **walkable, first-person** landscape (WASD + mouse-look);
34	    artifacts are embedded **in the terrain**, not floating on the globe. Walk up
35	    to one and press **E** to inspect; **B** leaves back to orbit.
36	  - Transition is a **crossfade cut** into a dedicated island scene (not a
37	    seamless dive onto the sphere).
38	  - Starting with **one island holding all the artifacts/puzzles**; more later.
39	
40	## Status
41	
42	### Done ✅ — the 3D world (user-approved)
43	- Procedural planet: lavender ocean, gold **metallic** islands (PBR
44	  metalness + low roughness + `RoomEnvironment` IBL → shimmer), soft frost
45	  poles, drifting clouds.
46	- Saturn-style banded ring (tilted, two gaps, transparent).
47	- Soft lavender fresnel atmosphere, violet-tinted starfield.
48	- Orbit + zoom controls; slow auto-rotation.
49	- Verified rendering in headless Chrome (WebGL2), no console errors.
50	
51	### Done ✅ — the two-level flow (2026-06-05)
52	- **Orbit view** (`planetView.js`): the planet plus a clean **HTML map pin**
53	  ("LANDING SITE") that tracks the island in screen space — no glow/beam. On
54	  hover a thin **outline ring** fades in on the surface and the pin lifts; click
55	  (pin or island) → crossfade → island. The island is found via a shared
56	  elevation sampler, and the **camera frames it front-and-centre on load**. Pin
57	  hides when the island rotates to the far side.
58	- **Island view** (`islandView.js`): a procedural **walkable terrain** island
59	  (radial-falloff heightmap, gold highlands, surrounded by lavender sea),
60	  lavender-dusk sky, soft warm sun. **First-person** controller (`firstPerson.js`,
61	  PointerLockControls + WASD, glued to the terrain, clamped to the island).
62	- The 4 artifacts (reusing the `debris.js` prop builders) sit **in the terrain**
63	  with tall findable light-beams; walk within range → "Press E to inspect" →
64	  opens the shared fragment panel. **B** returns to orbit.
65	- Verified both views render in headless Chrome (WebGL2), no console errors.
66	
67	### Not built yet ⏳
68	- Puzzle mechanics (panels are still lore stubs only).
69	- The command engine (see open questions).
70	- Win/lose + checkpoint-collection state.
71	- More islands (only one is built; orbit view shows a single pin).
72	- Polish backlog: bloom on gold glints, ring shadow cast on planet; island
73	  pass — props/landmarks so the terrain reads less like empty dunes, water
74	  shader, a proper skybox, third-person option if wanted; tune the in-terrain
75	  artifact beam tint (reads pink over the lavender sky).
76	
77	## Puzzle design (PROPOSED — not yet reviewed/built)
78	
79	Arc: **orient → restore → understand → escape**. Each puzzle is small: run a
80	command → read the recovered context → use one detail from it.
81	
82	| # | Fragment | Command | What's lost | Puzzle |
83	|---|----------|-----------|-------------|--------|
84	| 1 | 🪖 EVA Helmet | `recap` | "What was I doing before the crash?" | Run `recap`; read the summary of recent log entries; pick out the mission. |
85	| 2 | 📖 Torn Logbook | `checkpoint` | A setting got corrupted in the crash | Search checkpoints, find the last good one before the corruption, rewind to it. |
86	| 3 | 🖥️ Nav Panel | `activity` | "*When* did it go wrong?" | Read the activity timeline; find when the anomaly started. |
87	| 4 | 📡 Signal Beacon | `dispatch` | No way to call for help | Generate a dispatch summarizing all recovered context, broadcast it → **win**. |
88	
89	- **#4 is the ending**: you can only send a complete dispatch after recovering
90	  the other three. This quietly answers "how do you win / how do checkpoints
91	  accumulate."
92	
93	### Open questions (decide before/while building puzzles)
94	1. **Does the arc + mapping feel right?** (e.g. helmet → recap)
95	2. **Command engine:** simulated in-game terminal (portable, shareable web demo)
96	   vs. real CLI execution (authentic, needs a local backend) vs. hybrid.
97	   _Leaning simulated for a shareable demo; not yet decided._
98	3. **How literal is the command output?** Real-ish `entire` output vs. softened
99	   ship-AI flavor text.
100	4. **Win/lose model:** currently leaning "restore the ship's log" (collect all
101	   fragments, no hard lose state). Oxygen/timer and branching endings were
102	   other options.
103	
104	### Next step
105	Fully design **#1 (EVA Helmet / `recap`)** end-to-end as the template, then
106	clone the pattern to the other three.
107	
108	## Level 1 design — "First Memories" (agreed 2026-06-09)
109	
110	Framing inspiration: **Diner Dash**. The fun isn't the task, it's that every
111	action feeds a clear goal, each task is a short chain, a timer pushes you, and
112	you juggle toward a target. The three workflow beats map onto a Diner Dash
113	table:
114	
115	- **Do (recover/fix)** = take the order + cook
116	- **Freeze (commit)** = serve the food — locked in, but not scored yet
117	- **Checkpoint** = collect the check — *this is the step that banks progress*
118	
119	Key teaching point: in Diner Dash you can serve every table and score nothing if
120	you never collect. Same here — a frozen-but-not-checkpointed fix is a served
121	plate you never got paid for. **Freeze keeps it; checkpoint banks it.** The ship
122	rebuilds from checkpoints, not bare commits, so checkpoints literally ARE
123	forward progress.
124	
125	What a checkpoint shows (middle-ground detail — not the full real anatomy): a
126	real **12-char hex ID** (e.g. `711044b1fe29`, like real Entire checkpoints),
127	the commit **trailer** it's stamped with (`Entire-Checkpoint: <id>`), a
128	**one-line summary** of the fix, and a tiny
129	**who-did-what bar** (ship % / you %). Stands in for the real
130	transcript/prompts/token-usage/line-attribution without a spreadsheet. The ID
131	also appears stamped on the commit (ice block) so the link is visible.
132	
133	### Pressure: one level countdown (not per-memory)
134	A single **countdown clock** (top-left HUD, `TIME m:ss`) runs for the whole run
135	— tuned **scary-tight** (`TOTAL_TIME`, currently **45s** for 3 memories;
136	one-line tune in `islandView.js`). Bank every memory before it hits `0:00` or
137	the run **fails**: every un-banked memory **melts away** (sinks + fades, ice
138	included) and a "MEMORIES MELTED" screen offers **press R to try again** (full
139	reset). The clock escalates: **urgent** (red, pulsing) under 22s → **critical**
140	(frantic fast pulse + shake + glowing red digits) under 8s; it pauses while
141	you're in orbit. The **whole sky panics** too — starting at `PANIC_TIME` (22s)
142	the lavender dusk, fog, dome and sun lerp toward an angry **crimson**, eased so
143	it's barely perceptible at first and only fully reads in the last ~10s, with a
144	**throb** once critical (and held full-red behind the fail screen). One knob
145	(`PANIC_TIME` in `islandView.js`) moves the sky independently of the clock. The clock keeps running through the **final
146	`entire checkpoint list`** — that command is the real finish line, so banking
147	the last memory does NOT stop the clock; you still have to type the list before
148	`0:00` (and you can't Esc out of that final prompt). Time out there and the
149	whole run melts. This replaced the old per-memory ~14s fade — the user wanted
150	ONE clock and real pressure across the whole level, not individual items melting.
151	
152	### The loop (one memory at a time — calm tutorial, no juggling yet)
153	The player types the **real commands** into the ship's terminal (not abstract
154	keys). Walking up to a memory auto-opens an in-world command line (movement
155	freezes; keystrokes feed the terminal; Esc backs out; B returns to orbit).
156	Each step shows the exact command to type as a scaffold.
157	
158	1. A memory **surfaces** — light beam on the terrain.
159	2. Walk up → the **ship terminal opens** (`crashlog:~$`), hinting `git add`.
160	3. Type **`git add`** → memory is staged/recovered.
161	4. Type **`git commit`** → encased in **ice** (commit).
162	5. Entire then **offers to link a checkpoint** — `Link this commit to a
163	   checkpoint? [y/n]`. Press **`y`** → ice lights up, a floating real
164	   **12-char hex ID** (e.g. `711044b1fe29`) appears, the record card pops,
165	   **ship power ticks up**. (Decline with `n`
166	   and it stays an un-tracked commit — re-approach to link it later.)
167	6. Walk to the next memory.
168	7. When all are linked → **the clock is still ticking** → race to type
169	   **`entire checkpoint list`** before `0:00` to see every checkpoint you
170	   collected → ship fully restored (win). Miss it and the whole run melts.
171	
172	IMPORTANT accuracy note (user corrected this): you do NOT type `entire
173	checkpoint` to save — in real Entire, linking a checkpoint is a yes/no offer
174	made after a commit. `entire checkpoint list` is the real command, used at the
175	end to review what you've banked.
176	
177	~3 memories; tutorial scaffolds the first of each action, near-silent after.
178	Wrong commands get a "command not recognized — try: <cmd>" nudge.
179	
180	The make-it-click beats, taught via the countdown + the meter:
181	- the level **clock** is the pressure — anything not banked before `0:00` melts.
182	- `git commit` freezes it but **doesn't move the meter** — only linking the
183	  checkpoint (`y`) banks it. Teaches commit-vs-checkpoint, no "go back" mechanic.
184	
185	### Out of scope for L1 (later levels)
186	Juggling multiple memories / tighter timers; the "go back / reapply a checkpoint"
187	payoff; recap / activity / dispatch; win/lose beyond the power meter.
188	
189	## Level 2 design — "The Drone Bay" (agreed 2026-06-10, built 2026-06-10)
190	
191	**Design rule (user, 2026-06-09): one new command per level, and it must
192	visibly show the value of checkpoints.** Level 2's command is
193	**`entire checkpoint explain`**. Nothing else is new.
194	
195	After playtesting the built Archive level (below), Rizel stepped back to first
196	principles: ground each level in the day-to-day agentic workflow. The daily
197	arc is **delegate → review → accept**, and the game had no agent in it. So
198	Level 2 puts the player on the review side of delegation — the one part of
199	the loop only the human does.
200	
201	### The fiction
202	The ship is broken into **5 systems**, each a damaged work site scattered
203	across the island: ignition coils, nav core, long-range antenna, life support
204	scrubbers, landing struts. The ship gives you a **drone bay with 5 drones**
205	(one per job — no economy, no earning). Drones fix things fast, but the ship
206	won't power up work nobody can account for.
207	
208	### The loop (one countdown for the whole level)
209	1. **Assign**: walk to a broken site, press E → a drone flies out and works
210	   on it (visible work beam / sparks). You're free immediately.
211	2. **Player's choice**: babysit one drone at a time, or sprint site-to-site
212	   launching the whole fleet. Nothing forces parallelism — the clock makes it
213	   the obviously rational move (same principle as search: the tool isn't a
214	   gate, it's the rational choice). Five beams running at once while you do
215	   nothing is the level's money shot.
216	3. **Drone finishes** → the site seals under a checkpoint id. You weren't
217	   there; you don't know what it did.
218	4. **Review**: walk up to a finished site → the terminal opens **pre-filled**
219	   with `entire checkpoint explain <id>` — press Enter (no typing ids; you
220	   still SEE that real explain takes an id). A story card shows what was
221	   actually done: "replaced coolant pump · 3 attempts · 2 parts scavenged".
222	5. **Accept**: an **ADD TO SHIP** confirm appears (Y, matching L1's confirm
223	   beat) → that system comes online, ship meter +20%.
224	6. **Finish line**: the FIFTH accept keeps the terminal open — the next
225	   command happens at the prompt you're already at, like the real CLI. Type
226	   `entire dispatch` ("generate a dispatch summarizing recent agent work" —
227	   five drones just worked; the report writes itself from the checkpoints).
228	   `entire checkpoint list` still works there as an optional L1 callback and
229	   nudges you to dispatch. (Changed 2026-06-10 from "walk back to the console
230	   and run `list`" — Rizel couldn't find the console at the end; a final
231	   fetch-quest was friction, not tension, and dispatch is the truer end-of-day
232	   command. If the player wanders off, any online system or the bay console
233	   reopens the report prompt.)
234	
235	Fail = clock hits 0:00 before all five are accepted → R to retry.
236	
237	### Deliberately NOT in Level 2
238	No bad/botched drone work (no deduction, nothing to compare — explain is the
239	gate to the ADD TO SHIP button, not a puzzle), no drone management or upgrade
240	mechanics (more drones = parallelism, never new mechanics), no typing
241	checkpoint ids, no values to extract from explanations. The "one drone did it
242	wrong — find it" twist is reserved as a possible later level once this loop
243	is proven.
244	
245	### The upgrade table (drones don't repair — they IMPROVISE)
246	The transformation is what makes you *need* the explanation: you left a bent
247	dish, you come back to a lance pointed at the sky — "what did you DO?" is the
248	urge `explain` exists to satisfy.
249	
250	| System (broken) | Becomes | Explain card flavor |
251	|---|---|---|
252	| Ignition coils (charred leaning stack) | **Plasma Ring** — floating gold torus | "coils beyond saving — rebuilt as a plasma ring from salvaged hull plate · 2 attempts" |
253	| Nav core (cracked dark gyro) | **Star Dome** — projected starfield + orbiting ring | "core unrecoverable — remapped from scratch; starfield calibrated to the lavender belt" |
254	| Long-range antenna (dish face-down in the dirt) | **Signal Spire** — lance firing a beam to orbit | "dish unsalvageable — respun the mast into a spire · 3 attempts · the first two fell over" |
255	| Life support scrubbers (rusty vent box) | **Garden Pod** — glass dome, glowing plants | "filters dead — replaced with a living filter; two vines scavenged from the crash" |
256	| Landing struts (collapsed leg) | **Grav Skid** — hover pad bobbing over a glow ring | "strut seized solid — swapped for grav skids; technically the ship floats now" |
257	
258	Visual grammar (status readable from across the island via beam color):
259	amber beam = broken (blinking red warn bulb up close) → cyan pulsing beam +
260	hovering drone + work beam = drone at work → ice-blue beam + L1-style ice
261	seal + floating checkpoint id = finished, review me → no beam = accepted
262	(the upgrade itself is the landmark; ice melts, animations wake up).
263	
264	### The teaching, felt not told
265	What the level actually shows (Rizel's framing, 2026-06-10 — keep it this
266	way): **you can have multiple agents working in parallel, see what work each
267	one did, and get a summary at the end.** Sending a drone (E) is one button —
268	delegation is demonstrated as spectacle, not taught; ADD TO SHIP is just the
269	gate that makes reading the explanation non-skippable. The two things the
270	player genuinely learns are the commands: `entire checkpoint explain` (see
271	what an agent did while you weren't watching — the level's one taught
272	mechanic) and `entire dispatch` (the day, summarized — a ceremonial closer
273	with nothing to learn, the role `list` played in L1). Arc: L1 — bank it.
274	L2 — agents work, you can always see and summarize what they did.
275	Search/rewind/recap reserved for later levels, by which point the checkpoint
276	history will have grown naturally.
277	
278	### Implementation (2026-06-10)
279	Lives in `src/droneBayView.js`; HUD block `#db-hud` in `index.html`; styles
280	share L1's countdown/briefing/fail selectors. The shelved Archive level stays
281	fully playable at `?view=archive`; `?view=level2` / `?level=2` and the
282	post-L1 glitching pin now route to the Drone Bay. Specifics:
283	- 5 sites + 5 parked drones by the console (bay row at z=50, heights
284	  node-verified). Drones arc to the site (~26 u/s), hover-orbit while
285	  working (`WORK_TIME` 18s), then fly home. Work continues while the player
286	  is elsewhere — that's the point.
287	- One 150s clock (`TOTAL_TIME`); serial play (~35s/system × 5) can't beat it,
288	  the fleet can. Same panic-sky as L1.
289	- Fleet status panel (top-left): BROKEN / DRONE AT WORK / READY TO REVIEW /
290	  ONLINE per system.
291	- Review terminal auto-opens at a sealed site, pre-filled with
292	  `entire checkpoint explain <id>` — Enter runs it (no id typing), card rows
293	  print, then a green **ADD TO SHIP** button (clickable; Y also works).
294	- Finish line: the fifth accept rolls the same terminal into report mode;
295	  typed `entire dispatch` prints the day report (5 upgrades, "crew: 1 human,
296	  5 drones"), then the win screen. `entire checkpoint list` optional there.
297	- Fail at 0:00 → R resets everything (sites, drones, clock).
298	- Bird's-eye map (M, `src/overhead.js`) on all island levels — top-down
299	  camera + you-are-here arrow, walking still works, terminals open over it.
300	
301	## Level 3 design — "Launch Clearance" (agreed + built 2026-06-10 — name TBD, pending playtest)
302	
303	The final level. Designed across two sessions on 2026-06-10 (the morning
304	session's "anomaly squashing" draft evolved into this; rejected on the way:
305	"The Other Ship" dead-crew mystery — "good story but far too many details",
306	raw search box-checking — "eh", and symptom-matching — "how would they know").
307	Simplicity bar (Rizel): GitHub's Bug Bash — "all they do is squash bugs and
308	pick up lifepoints. simplicity."
309	
310	**The aha to deliver** (modeled on a real moment: Claude answered "what were
311	the level 3 plans?" from this repo's own checkpoint transcripts): you're asked
312	a question you provably can't answer from memory, and the record answers it.
313	L2 already manufactured the situation — the subagents worked while you weren't
314	watching. **Arc: L1 — bank your work. L2 — subagents work while you don't
315	watch. L3 — someone asks about that work; you weren't there, the record was.**
316	
317	### The fiction
318	The ship is repaired — now it has to fly. The player is **inside the ship,
319	in the pilot's chair** (first time aboard; alone signals "finale"). The launch
320	computer won't arm on work nobody can account for — the same rule the ship
321	enforced in L2, escalated to takeoff. The questioner is the **ship's AI: the
322	amnesiac from Level 1**, verifying against the memory the player banked for
323	it. First scene and last scene are the same character, before and after.
324	Briefing line (approved verbatim, keep it):
325	
326	> "I can read the record. Protocol says you have to be the one to confirm it."
327	
328	### The loop (whole level at one console — no walking)
329	~5 questions under one clock, constant shape, two clicks each:
330	1. A question appears in plain words — answerable **only from the record**:
331	   "The antenna repair — how many attempts did it take?"
332	2. The terminal offers **~3 tools as multiple choice** (click / number key) —
333	   e.g. `entire checkpoint explain <id>` / Skill: *what-happened* /
334	   `entire dispatch`.
335	3. It runs **visibly**, answering in that tool's voice: raw command → the full
336	   record card; a skill → visibly runs the command, then one plain sentence
337	   (the skills pitch, demonstrated not explained).
338	4. **Answer chips** ([2] [3] [5]) — the answer is on screen in the output.
339	   Zero typing, zero keyword guessing, zero memory.
340	5. Correct → a **launch-code segment locks** (▣ ▣ □ □ □), the system audibly
341	   arms in the cabin, the matching upgrade flares out on the island. Wrong →
342	   the card stays up, the clock keeps eating, click again.
343	6. 5/5 → code complete → countdown → **liftoff = the game's ending** (planet
344	   falls away, the labeled upgrades shrinking below). Win screen carries
345	   `npx skills add https://github.com/entireio/skills`.
346	
347	Fail = launch window missed at 0:00 → R to retry.
348	
349	### Tool-menu rules (Rizel's locked preferences)
350	- **Mostly ALL VALID, occasional dead end.** Usually 2 of 3 options genuinely
351	  answer it in different voices; one is a polite dead end that prints
352	  real-but-unhelpful output and costs only clock seconds (e.g. picking
353	  `explain` when you don't know *which* checkpoint — the fizzle teaches the
354	  search-vs-explain boundary). Never a fail state at the menu.
355	- **Menus ROTATE by question type** (never the same trio twice): what
356	  happened at one site → `explain` / Skill: *what-happened*; don't-know-where
357	  → `search` (the keyword comes from the question, never guessed — redeems
358	  the shelved Archive); order/when → `list` / `activity`; handoff flavor →
359	  Skill: *session-handoff* / *teach*; finale → `dispatch` (ceremonial closer,
360	  maybe no menu at all).
361	- **Small cast:** ~2–3 skills + 3–4 commands across the whole level — "we
362	  dont have to use every skill"; 11 skills would be a product tour.
363	- Possible easing: auto-run the tool on Q1–2, introduce the menu on Q3–5.
364	
365	### Deliberately NOT in Level 3
366	No typed search words, no free-text answers, no remembering things seen once
367	(every answer is on screen at the moment of choice), no fault-finding/blame
368	mechanic, no new mechanics past the two-click beat. Skills repo lives at
369	`~/Documents/work/skills` (11 skills) — only a few appear.
370	
371	### Open knobs (decide at build/playtest)
372	- Level name ("Launch Clearance" is a placeholder).
373	- Question count (~5) and which question types make the cut.
374	- The "discrepancy" question — one answer that surprises the player (grav
375	  skids: "torque spec: vibes") — safe cousin of the reserved "one drone did
376	  it wrong" twist. In or out?
377	- Trade-off to playtest: this is the least game-bodied level (terminal +
378	  cabin, island as backdrop) — fits the operator→delegator graduation, but
379	  compare against a variant with one short walk per question if it feels flat
380	  after the Drone Bay.
381	- How the cabin/console is staged in 3D (new interior view vs. dressed-up
382	  terminal overlay).
383	
384	### Implementation (2026-06-10)
385	Lives in `src/launchView.js`; HUD block `#lc-hud` in `index.html`; styles
386	share the countdown/briefing/win/fail selector groups. `?view=level3` /
387	`?level=3` dev shortcut; L2's `entire dispatch` (onComplete) opens the launch
388	window — the orbit pin then boards the ship. Build decisions on the knobs:
389	- **Staging:** fixed cockpit rig above the bay (eye height 19, node-verified
390	  sightlines to all five upgrades), simple slab window frame + glowing dash
391	  glued to the camera, idle sway. The L2 upgrades stand on the island, alive
392	  (exported `SYSTEMS` + `UPGRADE_BUILDERS` from droneBayView).
393	- **5 questions:** antenna attempts (explain / what-happened / dispatch dead
394	  end), hull plate (search / recall / explain dead end), record count (list /
395	  recall / search dead end), why-the-ship-floats — the discrepancy question
396	  IS in (explain / what-happened / list dead end), then `entire dispatch`
397	  files the flight log (single pre-filled Enter, ceremonial).
398	- Confirm → gold beam flare at that system + a launch-code segment locks
399	  (shows the checkpoint's first hex). Wrong chip: dimmed, clock keeps eating.
400	  Dead-end tool: output prints, option struck through, try another.
401	- Liftoff: ~9s climb-out — island falls away, sky lerps to space, stars fade
402	  in — then the LIFTOFF win screen with the `npx skills add` line.
403	- One 150s window (`TOTAL_TIME`), same low/critical/panic-sky grammar as
404	  L1/L2; fail = LAUNCH WINDOW MISSED → R resets everything.
405	
406	## Level ? design — "The Archive" (built 2026-06-09, SHELVED for a later level)
407	
408	Built as Level 2, then shelved 2026-06-10 after a playtest: the story carried
409	too much weight ("meh, it just feels like too much") and search is a
410	weeks-later pain, not a day-to-day one. The implementation is kept intact in
411	`src/archiveView.js`, playable at `?view=archive` — it should return as a
412	later search level, by which point the player's checkpoint history (incl.
413	drone work) will have grown enough that search needs no lore-dump. Its
414	command was **`entire checkpoint search`**.
415	
416	Rejected on the way here (kept for the record so we don't re-tread):
417	- An elaborate "corruption" level teaching search + explain + rewind with
418	  clue-hunting, decoy checkpoints, and a spreading corruption zone — **too many
419	  variables to consume at once**.
420	- `rewind` as the L2 command — in the simple framings it kept mis-modeling the
421	  tool (reading as "restore from backup" when real rewind means "take my
422	  *current* state back to a save point; the bank itself is never at risk").
423	- `recap` — L1's three collected items don't warrant a recap; manufacturing the
424	  need (more items, mixed states, a blackout) was creeping back toward
425	  variable-overload.
426	
427	### The fiction
428	Level 1's win restored the ship's memory — side effect: the ship's **entire
429	pre-crash checkpoint archive surfaces**. The island is now dotted with ~20
430	identical dark frozen memories (ice blocks, no beams, unreadable from a
431	distance). Most were never grabbed by the player — the corpus is deliberately
432	**bigger than your head**, because that's the situation search exists for.
433	The player's 3 L1 checkpoints can appear in the archive as a continuity touch.
434	
435	### The loop (×3, one countdown clock for tension)
436	1. **The ship asks** for a memory in a plain sentence that contains the
437	   keyword: *"I need the memory of the **ignition sequence**."* (No clue
438	   hunting — the search word is right there in the request.)
439	2. **Player types** `entire checkpoint search "ignition"` at the terminal.
440	3. **The matching block's beam lights up** across the island — the money shot:
441	   a dark field, one typed word, one light. (In L1 the game lit the beams for
442	   you; in L2 nothing lights until YOU search.)
443	4. **Sprint over, press E** → memory transmits to the ship, power meter
444	   climbs, next request.
445	
446	Wrong/misspelled word → 0 results, no penalty except the ticking clock (which
447	is exactly the real-world cost of bad search terms). Searching by walking the
448	field and inspecting blocks one-by-one stays *possible* but ruinously slow —
449	the tool isn't a gate, it's the obviously rational move.
450	
451	The teaching, felt not told: **your history quickly outgrows your memory;
452	you remember a *word*, not a place — search turns the word into the moment.**
453	Arc so far: L1 — bank it. L2 — search it. (recap / dispatch / resume / rewind
454	reserved for later levels.)
455	
456	### Deliberately NOT in Level 2
457	No clue collection, no decoy results, no timestamps, no `explain`, no rewind
458	browser, no new artifact states. The ~20 archive blocks are set dressing, not
459	state to track. Retrieval is a plain E-grab — the level's typing effort lives
460	in the search command itself (leaning: keep it that simple rather than rerun
461	L1's add/commit beat per item; revisit after a playtest).
462	
463	### Implementation (2026-06-09)
464	Lives in `src/archiveView.js` (the abandoned corruption level was stripped;
465	kept from that work: `src/memoryProps.js`, the `onComplete` hook in
466	`islandView.js`, the `#fp-shared` HUD split, the glitching-pin entry after L1
467	completes, and the `?view=level2` / `?level=2` dev shortcuts). Specifics:
468	- **21 archive blocks** (3 targets + 15 old-crew checkpoints + the 3 L1
469	  recoveries with the dev-scaffold ids), scattered deterministically on dry
470	  land (seeded RNG, min spacing, never in the sea or on the console).
471	- Blocks are dark and anonymous; an id sprite appears only when lit, grabbed,
472	  or walked up close (~18u) — browsing on foot stays possible but slow.
473	- The ship's request panel (top-left, under the clock) holds the keyword in a
474	  plain sentence. Terminal (gold beam, auto-opens like L1) accepts
475	  `entire checkpoint search "<word>"` and `entire checkpoint list` (prints all
476	  21 — "too many to read" — the why-search-exists beat).
477	- Search lights every match's cyan beam (previous search goes dark); E on the
478	  requested block transmits it (warm gold); E on a lit-but-wrong block costs
479	  only the re-read. 0 results cost only clock.
480	- One 90s countdown (tunable `TOTAL_TIME`), same panic-sky as L1, fail = R to
481	  retry, win = "ARCHIVE LINKED" + B to orbit.
482	
483	## Architecture / where things live
484	
485	```
486	index.html         # canvas + HUD + crossfade overlay + FP prompt + panel + loader
487	src/style.css      # HUD / panel / loader / fade / crosshair / FP-prompt styling
488	src/main.js        # VIEW MANAGER: owns renderer + resize + shared panel + the
489	                   #   render loop; crossfades between the two views.
490	                   #   ?view=island jumps straight onto the island (dev aid).
491	src/planetView.js  # orbit view: scene/lighting/stars/planet/clouds/atmo/ring +
492	                   #   the clickable gold landing hotspot. onIslandClick callback.
493	src/islandView.js  # LEVEL 1: sky/light, terrain+water, the memories, terminal
494	                   #   loop, countdown. enter()/exit()/onExit/onComplete.
495	src/droneBayView.js# LEVEL 2 ("The Drone Bay"): 5 broken systems, 5 drones,
496	                   #   pre-filled `entire checkpoint explain` + ADD TO SHIP.
497	                   #   Exports SYSTEMS + UPGRADE_BUILDERS for Level 3.
498	src/launchView.js  # LEVEL 3 ("Launch Clearance"): cockpit finale at one
499	                   #   console — ship AI asks, pick the tool (1/2/3), confirm
500	                   #   the answer, launch code fills, liftoff = the ending.
501	src/archiveView.js # SHELVED search level ("The Archive"), at ?view=archive:
502	                   #   ~21 dark blocks, ship requests, checkpoint search beat.
503	src/memoryProps.js # shared props: beam texture, ice block, id sprite, id gen
504	src/overhead.js    # bird's-eye map toggle (M) for all island levels: fixed
505	                   #   top-down camera + gold you-are-here arrow; walking
506	                   #   still works while overhead (fp alwaysMove flag)
507	src/terrain.js     # procedural island heightmap mesh + water + heightAt(x,z)
508	src/firstPerson.js # PointerLockControls + WASD walker, glued to the terrain
509	src/noise.js       # seedable 3D simplex + fBm (sphere-sampled → seamless)
510	src/planet.js      # bakes planet maps; createElevationSampler() finds land for
511	                   #   the hotspot. Palette constants (DEEP/SHALLOW/SNOW) here.
512	src/atmosphere.js  # fresnel limb-glow shell shader (orbit view)
513	src/ring.js        # procedural banded ring (radial-remapped UVs)
514	src/debris.js      # FRAGMENTS[] (lore + command) + exported prop BUILDERS,
515	                   #   reused as the island artifacts. createDebris() is now
516	                   #   unused (kept for reference / git history).
517	```
518	
519	Run: `npm install` then `npm run dev` → http://localhost:5173
520	Controls: orbit = drag/scroll, click the gold marker to land. Island = click to
521	capture mouse, WASD to walk, E to inspect a glowing artifact, B to leave.
522	
523	## History
524	Repo started as `signalkit` (a Python telemetry CLI), then pivoted to Planetfall
525	on 2026-06-05. The old code is recoverable via git history + Entire checkpoints.

## Planetfall — a 3D browser game that teaches the Entire checkpoint workflow

**What it is.** A Three.js + Vite game (no build assets — everything procedural) where a stranded astronaut restores their ship AI's lost memory. The fiction maps directly onto real Entire commands: restoring the ship's memory *is* the checkpoint workflow. The repo started life as `signalkit`, a Python telemetry CLI, and pivoted on June 5.

**The three-level arc** (all built, as of yesterday):

1. **First Memories** (`islandView.js`) — Diner Dash-style loop: walk to a glowing memory, `git add`, `git commit` (freezes it in ice), then accept Entire's `[y/n]` checkpoint-link offer to actually bank it. Finish with `entire checkpoint list` before a 45-second clock melts everything. Teaching: *freeze keeps it; checkpoint banks it.*
2. **The Drone Bay** (`droneBayView.js`) — five subagents repair five systems in parallel while you can only be in one place. Each finished job seals under a checkpoint; a pre-filled `entire checkpoint explain` shows what the drone actually did (they improvise — a bent dish comes back as a Signal Spire), then `entire dispatch` files the day's report.
3. **Launch Clearance** (`launchView.js`) — the cockpit finale, no walking. The ship AI asks five questions only the record can answer; you pick a tool from a rotating multiple-choice menu (commands and skills, mostly all-valid with the occasional dead end), confirm answers, fill the launch code, and lift off.

There's also a **shelved fourth level**, The Archive (`archiveView.js`, `?view=archive`) — a `checkpoint search` level built then pulled after a playtest, kept playable for later reuse.

**Architecture in one breath:** `main.js` is the view manager (renderer, crossfades, level progression); each level is a self-contained view module with `enter()/exit()/onComplete`; shared bits live in `memoryProps.js` (ice/beams/checkpoint ids), `firstPerson.js` (WASD walker), `overhead.js` (M-key map), and the procedural stack (`planet.js`, `terrain.js`, `noise.js`, `atmosphere.js`, `ring.js`). Dev shortcuts: `?view=island`, `?level=2`, `?level=3`, `?view=archive`.

**Current state:** working tree is clean against `main` — the only untracked thing is a `.codex/` directory (hooks config + an `entire-search` agent definition, from June 5). The most recent commits wrapped up Level 3, chained wins between levels, and refreshed the README to cover the full game. PLAN.md is meticulous — it records not just decisions but rejected designs (the corruption level, "The Other Ship", graphics overhauls) so they don't get re-trodden.

The game is feature-complete across all three levels; PLAN.md flags Level 3's name as a placeholder "pending playtest." Want me to run it, or dig into anything specific?

  "content": "import puppeteer from 'puppeteer-core';\n\nconst sleep = (ms) => new Promise((r) => setTimeout(r, ms));\n\nconst browser = await puppeteer.launch({\n  executablePath: '/Applications/Google Chrome.app/Contents/MacOS/Google Chrome',\n  headless: 'new',\n  args: ['--window-size=1440,900', '--hide-scrollbars'],\n  defaultViewport: { width: 1440, height: 900 },\n});\nconst page = await browser.newPage();\nawait page.goto('https://bug-bash.github.com/', { waitUntil: 'networkidle2', timeout: 60000 });\n\n// let the game boot and any intro animation play\nawait sleep(6000);\nawait page.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/bb-1-landing.png' });\n\n// log what's in the game container for context\nconst info = await page.evaluate(() => {\n  const c = document.querySelector('#game-container');\n  return c ? c.innerHTML.slice(0, 2000) : 'no #game-container';\n});\nconsole.log('CONTAINER:', info);\n\n// click center of the canvas / press keys that arcade games commonly use to advance\nconst canvas = await page.$('canvas');\nif (canvas) {\n  const box = await canvas.boundingBox();\n  await page.mouse.click(box.x + box.width / 2, box.y + box.height / 2);\n}\nawait sleep(2000);\nawait page.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/bb-2-after-click.png' });\n\nawait page.keyboard.press('Enter');\nawait sleep(2000);\nawait page.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/bb-3-after-enter.png' });\n\nawait page.keyboard.press('Space');\nawait sleep(3000);\nawait page.screenshot({ path: '/tmp/bb-4-after-space.png' });\n\nawait browser.close();\nconsole.log('done');\n"
}

}

  "content": "---\nname: reference-bug-bash-ux\ndescription: UX breakdown of Mona's Bug Bash (bug-bash.github.com) — Rizel's simplicity bar; arcade-TV framing and minimal onboarding details\nmetadata:\n  type: reference\n---\n\nhttps://bug-bash.github.com/ — GitHub Design's \"Mona's Bug Bash\", the game Rizel\ncites as the simplicity bar (see [[level3-anomaly-design]]). Playtested headlessly\n2026-06-11; key UX facts:\n\n- Page = dark room + centered rounded-corner canvas styled like a CRT TV; zero\n  instructions on the page itself. Theater/fullscreen corner buttons only.\n- Arcade feel = `image-rendering: pixelated` + chromatic aberration (RGB fringe)\n  + scanlines + vignette/bezel + grey \"phosphor\" scene fades. Cheap post effects,\n  not asset-heavy.\n- Onboarding: title menu (Start/Options/Leaderboard/Credits) → 4 one-line\n  dialogue beats (Space to advance) that ARE the story → goal in one sentence\n  (\"Help Mona squash the bugs before time runs out!\") → controls in one\n  parenthetical line → lights on, Time: 60, play. ~15 seconds total.\n- One UI channel (bottom dialogue box) carries story+goal+controls; HUD is\n  hearts + score + countdown, all self-explanatory arcade grammar.\n\nRelevant to Planetfall: it front-loads far less text than our briefings; the\nTV-bezel treatment would be cheap if Rizel ever wants it (but see\n[[graphics-overhaul-rejected]] — don't add unasked).\n"
}

That's the full picture — summary above stands, and I've saved the Bug Bash UX notes to memory for future design conversations. The three things it does that are most relevant to compare against Planetfall: the page-as-dark-room-with-a-TV framing, the ~15-second all-in-fiction onboarding (story, goal, and controls each get exactly one line in one dialogue box), and the cheap CRT post-effects (pixelated rendering, chromatic fringe, scanlines, bezel vignette) doing all the genre-setting before a single word is read.

> AGENT

I agree with your instincts, and I'd push them one step further: the thing that makes Bug Bash's onboarding work isn't *where* the text is, it's that the story, the goal, and the controls all arrive through **one character, one box, one line at a time**. We already have that character — the ship AI. It's the amnesiac in L1 and the questioner in L3, but right now it doesn't actually *talk* to you in between. Here's how I'd rank the ideas:

## 1. Ship-AI dialogue beats replace the briefing panels (do this first)

Our current briefings are paragraph-style panels with a CONTROLS section — the player reads a wall, then plays. Swap each one for 3–5 one-line beats advanced with Space, in the ship AI's voice, always ending with the same two-line shape: **one goal sentence, one controls line.** Sketch for L1:

> *"...hello? Someone's out there. I can't remember anything."*
> *"My memory is scattered across this island. I can see the pieces glowing."*
> *"Freeze them, then link them to me — frozen isn't saved. Saved is saved."*
> **"Bank all three memories before the clock hits 0:00."**
> *(WASD to walk · walk up to a glow and type what the terminal shows)*

This also fixes a structural thing for free: the ship AI gains personality level by level as its memory returns — confused in L1, businesslike in L2, fully itself asking questions in L3. The finale's "I can read the record. Protocol says you have to be the one to confirm it" lands much harder if you've watched this voice come back to life. And the win→`Enter` chaining we already built is the natural place for one connective story beat between levels.

## 2. A real title screen (your "landing page" idea — yes)

Right now you land in orbit with no ceremony. Give it the arcade boot: the orbit view already running as the backdrop (exactly like Bug Bash's lab behind the logo), **PLANETFALL** in big type, and a tiny menu — `▸ Begin` / maybe `Levels` for the dev shortcuts. The story hook is one line under the logo: *"Your ship's AI has lost its memory."* Nothing else. The planet slowly rotating behind a title card is already a strong attract screen — we built it, we're just not using it as one.

## 3. TV framing — but as the *terminal's* skin, not the page's

Here's where I'd deviate from Bug Bash. Their CRT treatment works because the whole game is pixel art — scanlines and chromatic fringe over our soft lavender 3D world would fight the look (and it's adjacent to the graphics-overhaul territory we decided to stay out of). But the *terminal* is diegetically a crashed ship's display — scanlines, a faint flicker, a curved-glass vignette on the terminal overlay and dialogue boxes would be cheap CSS, would make every text moment feel like ship hardware, and the world stays clean. The "arcade TV" feeling gets attached to the thing the player reads, which is exactly where you want their attention anyway.

If we ever host it on a real page, the Bug Bash page model (dark room, framed canvas, title + one footer line, zero instructions outside the screen) is the right call there too — but that's a distribution question, not a game change.

## What I'd skip

Pixelated rendering, hearts/score HUD, leaderboards — those are Bug Bash being an arcade brawler. Our HUD grammar (clock, meter, fleet panel) is already self-explanatory the way their hearts are.

My recommendation on order: **dialogue beats first** (it touches all three levels and is mostly copy + a reusable beat-box component), **title screen second**, **terminal CRT skin third** (pure polish, no design risk). Want me to draft the actual beat scripts for all three levels so you can react to the writing before we build anything?

97	// ---------- views ----------
98	// After Level 1's `entire checkpoint list`, the ship wakes its drone bay:
99	// the orbit pin glitches and landing again enters Level 2 ("The Drone Bay").
100	// After Level 2's `entire dispatch`, the launch window opens: landing again
101	// enters Level 3 ("Launch Clearance") — the finale.
102	// The shelved search level ("The Archive") stays reachable at ?view=archive.
103	let level1Done = jumpToLevel2 || jumpToLevel3;
104	let level2Done = jumpToLevel3;
105	
106	const planetView = createPlanetView(renderer, {
107	  onIslandClick: () => switchTo(
108	    level2Done ? launchView : level1Done ? droneBayView : islandView
109	  ),
110	});
111	// Success carries you forward (onNext); failure only ever offers R to retry.
112	const islandView = createIslandView(renderer, {
113	  onExit: () => switchTo(planetView),
114	  onComplete: () => { level1Done = true; },
115	  onNext: () => switchTo(droneBayView),
116	});
117	const droneBayView = createDroneBayView(renderer, {
118	  onExit: () => switchTo(planetView),
119	  onComplete: () => { level2Done = true; },
120	  onNext: () => switchTo(launchView),

122	const archiveView = createArchiveView(renderer, {
123	  onExit: () => switchTo(planetView),
124	});
125	const launchView = createLaunchView(renderer, {

127	});

129	// Default to the orbit view; ?view=island jumps straight to Level 1,
130	// ?view=level2 (or ?level=2) to Level 2, ?view=level3 (or ?level=3) to the
131	// finale, ?view=archive to the shelved search level — handy for development.
132	let current = requestedView === "island" ? islandView
133	  : requestedView === "archive" ? archiveView
134	  : jumpToLevel3 ? launchView
135	  : jumpToLevel2 ? droneBayView : planetView;
136	current.enter();

144	function refreshOrbitHud() {
145	  hint.classList.toggle("hidden", current !== planetView);
146	  hint.textContent = level2Done
147	    ? "The launch window is open — the ship is asking for you. Click the pin to board"
148	    : level1Done
149	    ? "A new signal — the ship's drone bay just woke up. Click the pin to land"
150	    : "Drag to orbit · Scroll to zoom · Click the pin to land";
151	  pin?.classList.toggle("is-corrupted", level1Done && !level2Done);
152	}
153	refreshOrbitHud();

155	function switchTo(view) {
156	  if (transitioning || view === current) return;
157	  transitioning = true;
158	  fade.classList.add("show");
159	  setTimeout(() => {

161	    current = view;
162	    current.enter();
163	    refreshOrbitHud();
164	    fade.classList.remove("show");
165	    transitioning = false;
166	  }, 650); // match #fade CSS transition

346	/* Critical state — under a few seconds, the clock goes frantic */
347	#countdown.is-critical,
348	#l2-countdown.is-critical,
349	#db-countdown.is-critical,
350	#lc-countdown.is-critical {
351	  border-color: rgba(255, 60, 60, 0.95);
352	  background: rgba(60, 8, 10, 0.72);
353	  animation: cd-panic 0.5s steps(2, end) infinite;
354	}
355	#countdown.is-critical .cd-label,
356	#l2-countdown.is-critical .cd-label,
357	#db-countdown.is-critical .cd-label,
358	#lc-countdown.is-critical .cd-label { color: #ff4d4d; }
359	#countdown.is-critical #countdown-time,
360	#l2-countdown.is-critical #l2-countdown-time,
361	#db-countdown.is-critical #db-countdown-time,
362	#lc-countdown.is-critical #lc-countdown-time {
363	  color: #ff5a4d;
364	  text-shadow: 0 0 12px rgba(255, 70, 60, 0.9);
365	}
366	
367	@keyframes cd-panic {
368	  0% { box-shadow: 0 0 22px rgba(255, 50, 50, 0.8); transform: translateX(-1px); }
369	  100% { box-shadow: 0 0 8px rgba(255, 50, 50, 0.4); transform: translateX(1px); }
370	}

372	/* Time-out fail screen */
373	/* ---------- landing briefing modal ---------- */
374	#briefing,
375	#l2-briefing,
376	#db-briefing,
377	#lc-briefing {
378	  position: absolute;
379	  inset: 0;

386	  background: radial-gradient(ellipse at 50% 30%, rgba(20, 16, 44, 0.62), rgba(2, 4, 10, 0.86));
387	  backdrop-filter: blur(7px);

391	#l2-briefing.hidden,

397	  to { opacity: 1; }

984	}
985	#db-add-btn:active { transform: translateY(0); }

987	/* `entire checkpoint list` / search output. Level 2's full archive listing is
988	   long on purpose — it scrolls, and that's the lesson. */
989	#term-list:not(.hidden) {
990	  display: flex;
991	  flex-direction: column;
992	  gap: 5px;
993	  margin-top: 11px;
994	  padding-top: 10px;
995	  border-top: 1px solid rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.16);
996	  max-height: 168px;
997	  overflow-y: auto;
998	}
999	.term-list-row {
1000	  display: flex;
1001	  gap: 12px;
1002	  font-size: 12.5px;
1003	  line-height: 1.3;
1004	}
1005	.tl-id { color: var(--accent); min-width: 300px; white-space: nowrap; }
1006	.tl-key { color: var(--ink); opacity: 0.55; }
1007	.tl-title { color: var(--ink); opacity: 0.82; }
1008	
1009	/* Level 2 archive rows: just id + summary, so the id column stays compact. */
1010	.tl-id.tl-id-short { min-width: 110px; }
1011	/* Explain output rows: key/value pairs (Drone Bay review cards). */
1012	.tl-exp-key { min-width: 90px; flex: none; }
1013	
1014	.term-cursor {
1015	  display: inline-block;
1016	  width: 8px;
1017	  height: 16px;
1018	  background: var(--accent);
1019	  animation: term-blink 1s steps(1) infinite;
1020	}
1021	
1022	@keyframes term-blink { 50% { opacity: 0; } }
1023	
1024	#term-msg {
1025	  min-height: 13px;
1026	  margin-top: 9px;
1027	  font-size: 11.5px;
1028	  letter-spacing: 0.02em;
1029	  opacity: 0;
1030	  transition: opacity 0.15s ease;
1031	}
1032	#term-msg.show-ok { opacity: 0.92; color: #7cffb0; }
1033	#term-msg.show-err { opacity: 0.92; color: #ff8a73; }
1034	
1035	/* Map pin marking the landable island */
1036	#island-pin {
1037	  position: fixed;
1038	  top: 0; left: 0;
1039	  transform: translate(-50%, -100%);
1040	  padding: 0;
1041	  background: none;
1042	  border: none;
1043	  cursor: pointer;
1044	  pointer-events: auto;
1045	  z-index: 15;
1046	  transition: filter 0.2s ease, transform 0.18s cubic-bezier(0.22, 1, 0.36, 1);
1047	  transform-origin: bottom center;
1048	  filter:
1049	    drop-shadow(0 2px 4px var(--pin-shadow))
1050	    drop-shadow(0 0 6px rgba(255, 184, 107, 0.3));
1051	}
1052	#island-pin .pin-svg { display: block; }
1053	#island-pin .pin-svg path {
1054	  fill: var(--pin-shell);
1055	  stroke: var(--pin-rim);
1056	  stroke-width: 1.35;
1057	}
1058	#island-pin .pin-svg circle {
1059	  fill: var(--pin-core);
1060	}
1061	/* Hover (or keyboard focus, or synced from the 3D region) lifts the pin. */
1062	#island-pin:hover,
1063	#island-pin:focus-visible,
1064	#island-pin.is-hot {
1065	  transform: translate(-50%, -100%) scale(1.12);
1066	  filter:
1067	    drop-shadow(0 3px 5px var(--pin-shadow))
1068	    drop-shadow(0 0 12px rgba(255, 184, 107, 0.62));
1069	  outline: none;
1070	}
1071	
1072	/* After Level 1, the island's signal corrupts — the pin glitches magenta. */
1073	#island-pin.is-corrupted .pin-svg circle { fill: #ff2bd6; }
1074	#island-pin.is-corrupted .pin-svg path { stroke: rgba(255, 138, 216, 0.9); }
1075	#island-pin.is-corrupted {
1076	  filter:
1077	    drop-shadow(0 2px 4px var(--pin-shadow))
1078	    drop-shadow(0 0 10px rgba(255, 43, 214, 0.7));
1079	  animation: pin-glitch 2.2s steps(2, end) infinite;
1080	}
1081	@keyframes pin-glitch {
1082	  0%, 88% { transform: translate(-50%, -100%); }
1083	  90% { transform: translate(calc(-50% - 2px), -100%) skewX(6deg); }
1084	  94% { transform: translate(calc(-50% + 2px), -100%) skewX(-5deg); }
1085	  97%, 100% { transform: translate(-50%, -100%); }
1086	}
1087	
1088	/* Crossfade overlay between views */
1089	#fade {
1090	  position: fixed;
1091	  inset: 0;
1092	  background: #07050f;
1093	  opacity: 0;
1094	  pointer-events: none;
1095	  z-index: 40;
1096	  transition: opacity 0.65s ease;
1097	}
1098	#fade.show { opacity: 1; }

1339	/* Loader */
1340	#loader {
1341	  position: fixed;
1342	  inset: 0;
1343	  display: flex;
1344	  flex-direction: column;
1345	  align-items: center;
1346	  justify-content: center;
1347	  gap: 22px;
1348	  background: #02040a;
1349	  z-index: 50;
1350	  transition: opacity 0.8s ease;
1351	}
1352	
1353	#loader.done {
1354	  opacity: 0;
1355	  pointer-events: none;
1356	}
1357	
1358	.loader-ring {
1359	  width: 46px;
1360	  height: 46px;
1361	  border: 2px solid rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.2);
1362	  border-top-color: var(--accent);
1363	  border-radius: 50%;
1364	  animation: spin 0.9s linear infinite;
1365	}
1366	
1367	.loader-text {
1368	  font-size: 12px;
1369	  letter-spacing: 0.35em;
1370	  opacity: 0.7;
1371	}
1372	
1373	@keyframes spin { to { transform: rotate(360deg); } }
1374	
1375	.hidden { display: none; }

1377	/* ---------- Level 3 HUD ("Launch Clearance") ---------- */
1378	
1379	/* The briefing quotes the ship's AI — set the line apart. */
1380	.bf-quote {
1381	  font-family: ui-monospace, "SF Mono", Menlo, monospace;
1382	  font-size: 12.5px;
1383	  color: var(--accent);

1385	  padding-left: 12px;
1386	  margin-top: 10px;
1387	}
1388	
1389	/* The launch code — one segment per confirmed answer */
1390	#lc-code {
1391	  position: absolute;
1392	  top: 136px;
1393	  left: 32px;
1394	  padding: 12px 14px;
1395	  background: rgba(6, 11, 22, 0.78);
1396	  border: 1px solid rgba(255, 210, 122, 0.4);
1397	  border-radius: 9px;

1399	}
1400	.lc-code-head {
1401	  font-size: 10px;
1402	  letter-spacing: 0.22em;
1403	  font-weight: 700;
1404	  color: var(--accent-warm);
1405	  margin-bottom: 9px;
1406	}
1407	#lc-code-segs {
1408	  display: flex;
1409	  gap: 6px;
1410	}
1411	.lc-seg {
1412	  display: inline-grid;
1413	  place-items: center;
1414	  min-width: 44px;
1415	  height: 26px;
1416	  font-family: ui-monospace, "SF Mono", Menlo, monospace;
1417	  font-size: 12px;
1418	  letter-spacing: 0.08em;
1419	  color: var(--ink);
1420	  opacity: 0.4;
1421	  border: 1px dashed rgba(232, 244, 255, 0.35);
1422	  border-radius: 5px;
1423	}
1424	.lc-seg.is-locked {
1425	  opacity: 1;
1426	  color: #1a1206;
1427	  font-weight: 700;
1428	  border: none;

1430	  box-shadow: 0 0 14px rgba(255, 210, 122, 0.5);

1451	#lc-speaker {

1465	/* The tool menu — pick a way to look it up */

1517	/* What the tool printed */

1598	/* The finale: one pre-filled command, one Enter */
1599	.lc-single {
1600	  display: flex;

  "content": "// Title screen — the arcade boot menu shown over the orbit view on first\n// load. START GAME dismisses it; OPTIONS holds CONTROLS and SOUND. Sound\n// drives the existing #audio-panel controls (the canonical music state) so\n// this menu and the in-game panel can never disagree.\nexport function createTitleScreen({ onStart } = {}) {\n  const root = document.getElementById(\"title-screen\");\n  const screens = {\n    main: document.getElementById(\"ts-main\"),\n    options: document.getElementById(\"ts-options\"),\n    controls: document.getElementById(\"ts-controls\"),\n    sound: document.getElementById(\"ts-sound\"),\n  };\n  const parentOf = { options: \"main\", controls: \"options\", sound: \"options\" };\n\n  const bgm = document.getElementById(\"bgm\");\n  const audioToggle = document.getElementById(\"audio-toggle\");\n  const audioVolume = document.getElementById(\"audio-volume\");\n  const musicState = document.getElementById(\"ts-music-state\");\n  const volume = document.getElementById(\"ts-volume\");\n  const volumePct = document.getElementById(\"ts-volume-pct\");\n\n  let active = false;\n  let screenName = \"main\";\n  let items = [];\n  let sel = 0;\n\n  function syncSound() {\n    if (!bgm) return;\n    const playing = !bgm.paused;\n    musicState.textContent = playing ? \"ON\" : \"OFF\";\n    musicState.classList.toggle(\"is-off\", !playing);\n    volume.value = String(bgm.volume);\n    volumePct.textContent = `${Math.round(bgm.volume * 100)}%`;\n  }\n  bgm?.addEventListener(\"play\", syncSound);\n  bgm?.addEventListener(\"pause\", syncSound);\n  bgm?.addEventListener(\"volumechange\", syncSound);\n\n  function setVolume(v) {\n    const clamped = Math.min(1, Math.max(0, v));\n    if (audioVolume) {\n      // route through the in-game slider so its handler applies + reflects it\n      audioVolume.value = String(clamped);\n      audioVolume.dispatchEvent(new Event(\"input\"));\n    } else if (bgm) {\n      bgm.volume = clamped;\n    }\n  }\n\n  function toggleMusic() {\n    if (audioToggle) audioToggle.click();\n    else if (bgm) bgm.paused ? bgm.play().catch(() => {}) : bgm.pause();\n  }\n\n  function setSel(i) {\n    if (!items.length) return;\n    sel = (i + items.length) % items.length;\n    items.forEach((el, idx) => el.classList.toggle(\"is-selected\", idx === sel));\n  }\n\n  function setScreen(name) {\n    screenName = name;\n    for (const [key, el] of Object.entries(screens)) {\n      el.classList.toggle(\"hidden\", key !== name);\n    }\n    items = [...screens[name].querySelectorAll(\".ts-item\")];\n    setSel(0);\n    if (name === \"sound\") syncSound();\n  }\n\n  function back() {\n    if (parentOf[screenName]) setScreen(parentOf[screenName]);\n  }\n\n  function activate(el) {\n    switch (el?.dataset.action) {\n      case \"start\": hide(); onStart?.(); break;\n      case \"options\": setScreen(\"options\"); break;\n      case \"controls\": setScreen(\"controls\"); break;\n      case \"sound\": setScreen(\"sound\"); break;\n      case \"music-toggle\": toggleMusic(); break;\n      case \"back\": back(); break;\n    }\n  }\n\n  function onKey(e) {\n    if (!active) return;\n    const item = items[sel];\n    const onVolume = item?.dataset.action === \"volume\";\n    switch (e.key) {\n      case \"ArrowUp\": case \"w\": case \"W\": setSel(sel - 1); break;\n      case \"ArrowDown\": case \"s\": case \"S\": setSel(sel + 1); break;\n      case \"Enter\": case \" \": activate(item); break;\n      case \"Escape\": back(); break;\n      case \"ArrowLeft\":\n        if (!onVolume) return;\n        setVolume(Number(volume.value) - 0.05);\n        break;\n      case \"ArrowRight\":\n        if (!onVolume) return;\n        setVolume(Number(volume.value) + 0.05);\n        break;\n      default: return;\n    }\n    e.preventDefault();\n  }\n  window.addEventListener(\"keydown\", onKey);\n\n  for (const el of root.querySelectorAll(\".ts-item\")) {\n    el.addEventListener(\"mouseenter\", () => {\n      const idx = items.indexOf(el);\n      if (idx >= 0) setSel(idx);\n    });\n    el.addEventListener(\"click\", (e) => {\n      if (e.target === volume) return; // slider drag, not a menu pick\n      const idx = items.indexOf(el);\n      if (idx >= 0) setSel(idx);\n      activate(el);\n    });\n  }\n  volume?.addEventListener(\"input\", () => setVolume(Number(volume.value)));\n\n  function show() {\n    active = true;\n    root.classList.remove(\"hidden\", \"is-leaving\");\n    document.body.classList.add(\"title-up\");\n    setScreen(\"main\");\n    syncSound();\n  }\n\n  function hide() {\n    active = false;\n    document.body.classList.remove(\"title-up\");\n    root.classList.add(\"is-leaving\");\n    setTimeout(() => root.classList.add(\"hidden\"), 650); // match the CSS fade\n  }\n\n  return { show };\n}\n"
}

}\n\n/* While the title is up, the in-game chrome stays out of the shot. */\nbody.title-up #hud,\nbody.title-up #hint,\nbody.title-up #audio-panel,\nbody.title-up #island-pin { display: none !important; }\n\n.ts-logo {\n  font-size: clamp(40px, 7vw, 66px);\n  letter-spacing: 0.42em;\n  margin-right: -0.42em; /* optical centering: tracking pads the right edge */\n  font-weight: 600;\n  text-shadow: 0 0 28px rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.65), 0 0 80px rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.25);\n}\n\n.ts-tag {\n  margin-top: 16px;\n  font-size: 12px;\n  letter-spacing: 0.3em;\n  margin-right: -0.3em;\n  opacity: 0.62;\n}\n\n.ts-menu {\n  margin-top: 52px;\n  display: flex;\n  flex-direction: column;\n  align-items: center;\n  gap: 6px;\n}\n\n.ts-item {\n  position: relative;\n  padding: 7px 26px;\n  background: none;\n  border: none;\n  font-family: inherit;\n  font-size: 16px;\n  font-weight: 600;\n  letter-spacing: 0.26em;\n  color: var(--ink);\n  opacity: 0.7;\n  cursor: pointer;\n  transition: opacity 0.15s ease, color 0.15s ease;\n}\n.ts-item.is-selected {\n  color: var(--accent);\n  opacity: 1;\n  text-shadow: 0 0 16px rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.55);\n  outline: none;\n}\n.ts-item.is-selected::before {\n  content: \"▸\";\n  position: absolute;\n  left: 6px;\n  top: 50%;\n  transform: translateY(-50%);\n}\n.ts-item:focus-visible { outline: none; }\n\n/* Options panels (controls list, sound) */\n.ts-panel {\n  margin-top: 42px;\n  width: min(440px, 92vw);\n  max-height: 60vh;\n  overflow-y: auto;\n  padding: 22px 26px 16px;\n  background: var(--panel-bg);\n  border: 1px solid rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.28);\n  border-radius: 14px;\n  box-shadow: 0 26px 80px rgba(2, 4, 10, 0.6), 0 0 40px rgba(111, 227, 255, 0.1);\n  backdrop-filter: blur(7px);\n}\n.ts-group + .ts-group { margin-top: 16px; }\n.ts-group-head {\n  font-size: 10px;\n  letter-spacing: 0.24em;\n  font-weight: 700;\n  color: var(--accent-warm);\n  margin-bottom: 10px;\n}\n.ts-ctrl {\n  display: flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  gap: 8px;\n  padding: 3px 0;\n  font-size: 12.5px;\n  letter-spacing: 0.04em;\n  color: var(--ink);\n  opacity: 0.9;\n}\n.ts-panel .ts-item {\n  font-size: 13px;\n  letter-spacing: 0.18em;\n}\n.ts-panel-back {\n  display: block;\n  margin: 14px auto 0;\n}\n\n/* Sound rows: MUSIC ··· ON / VOLUME [slider] 55% */\n.ts-row {\n  display: flex;\n  align-items: center;\n  justify-content: space-between;\n  gap: 14px;\n  width: 100%;\n  padding: 9px 12px 9px 22px;\n  text-align: left;\n}\n.ts-value {\n  color: var(--accent);\n  font-weight: 700;\n  font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums;\n}\n.ts-value.is-off { color: var(--accent-warm); }\n#ts-volume {\n  width: 140px;\n  margin-left: auto;\n  accent-color: var(--accent-warm);\n  cursor: pointer;\n}\n#ts-volume-pct { min-width: 44px; text-align: right; }\n\n.ts-hint {\n  margin-top: 44px;\n  font-size: 11px;\n  letter-spacing: 0.1em;\n  opacity: 0.55;\n}\n\n@media (max-width: 680px) {\n  .ts-menu { margin-top: 38px; > AGENT

The title screen is built and verified. Here's what's in place:

**What it does**
- On a clean boot the game now opens to an arcade menu over the live orbit view — the rotating planet is the attract backdrop, Bug Bash style. Big **PLANETFALL** logo, the one-line hook *"YOUR SHIP'S AI HAS LOST ITS MEMORY"*, then **START GAME / OPTIONS**.
- **Options → Controls** shows the full key list grouped by context (In Orbit / On the Island / In the Cockpit), using the same key-chip styling as the briefings.
- **Options → Sound** has exactly what you asked for: **MUSIC ON/OFF** and a **VOLUME** slider. Both are wired *through* the existing in-game audio panel, so the title menu and the corner widget can never disagree — I verified a volume change in the menu lands on the music element, the in-game slider, and the menu's own display simultaneously.
- Navigation is full arcade grammar: ↑/↓ move the ▸ cursor, Enter selects, Esc backs out, ←/→ nudge the volume row — and mouse hover/click works everywhere too.
- The dev shortcuts (`?view=`, `?level=`) skip it, and the in-game chrome (small logo, hint, audio panel, landing pin) stays hidden until you press start. Nice side effect: the first menu press is the browser gesture that unblocks music autoplay, so "press start" genuinely starts the soundtrack.

**Where it lives:** `src/titleScreen.js` (new), markup in `index.html`, styles in `style.css`, two-line hookup in `main.js`. README and PLAN.md are updated — PLAN also records the two Bug Bash ideas we discussed but haven't built yet (ship-AI dialogue beats, terminal-scoped CRT skin) so they don't get lost.

I tested the whole flow in headless Chrome: boot → title → Options → Controls → back → Sound → music off (label flips, audio pauses) → volume nudges → Esc out → START GAME → title fades, orbit HUD returns. Screenshots are at `/tmp/ts-1-title.png` through `/tmp/ts-7-started.png` if you want to look before playing it yourself with `npm run dev`.

Nothing is committed yet — say the word if you want it on `main`.

Both fixed and verified:

1. **Key legend removed** — the "↑ ↓ choose · Enter select · Esc back" line at the bottom is gone (keyboard navigation still works, it's just not advertised; everything is clickable).
2. **Readability** — the overlay vignette is much deeper now (the planet dims to a backdrop instead of glowing through the text), and the logo, tagline, and menu items all got a dark halo behind them. The tagline and unselected items also sit at higher opacity. As you can see in the screenshots, START GAME / OPTIONS and the sound panel now read cleanly instead of fighting the lavender glow.

The trade-off I made: the planet is noticeably dimmer during the title screen than in-game — it brightens to full when you press START GAME, which actually works as a nice "waking up" beat. okay let me talk to you about the story i have in my mind. it's more like in the beginning was the software development lifecycle or like some kind of planet that supported the software development lifecycle..but the world has evolved and now the world has agents and humans collaborating. before it was just humans..but the old planet doesnt have enough support for agent collaboration..so youre moving to a new planet where things just work..you fly away in a spaceship but your spaceship breaks down. you need to bring items back on board, get system piece working again, and put your spaceship back in the mode to be able to fly..then fly away..okay so this story is not that good..but that's kinda like what im getting at..because entire is a cli tool meant to replace github ..we dont want to say that cuz all the features arent implemented yet but thats our ultimate goal..can you help me with the story a bit more

> AGENT

Your story is closer than you think — the migration idea is genuinely good, because it's Entire's actual pitch wearing a space suit: *the old world was built for humans working alone; work changed; the infrastructure has to change with it.* That says "we're the successor" without ever naming GitHub. Two things in the sketch are working against you, and both have clean fixes.

**Fix 1: The old planet isn't bad — it's outgrown.** "Old planet doesn't support agents" framed as a deficiency reads as trash-talk, and you don't want that (and can't back it yet). Frame it as an era ending instead: the old world was *great* at what it was built for. It kept every line of code ever written. What it never kept was the *moment* — what happened, who did it, why. That never mattered when every line was typed by a human who remembered. Then agents arrived, doing work nobody watched, and suddenly the thing the old world never stored is the thing you can't live without. Nobody's villainous. The world just changed. (This is also factually fair to git/GitHub: they keep the *what*, Entire keeps the *what happened*.)

**Fix 2: The breakdown needs a cause — and the cause should BE the lesson.** Right now the ship breaks "because the plot needs it." But you already built the perfect cause into the game: **the ship's amnesia.** Connect them:

> Your ship was built in the old world. It carried all your code — and no memory of how any of it came to be. One bad jump, the ship's mind faults, and there's nothing to rebuild from. The code survived the crash. The context didn't. That's why you're stranded.

Now the crash isn't an accident — it's a demonstration of the old way failing. The whole game becomes: rebuilding the ship *the new way*, where every piece of work is banked, explainable, and reportable. And the liftoff lands as a thesis statement: **the rebuilt ship is the first thing you've ever owned that flies on its record.** The launch computer arming off checkpoints (your existing L3!) is literally the new world's law, enforced one level early.

So the tightened story, in beats:

1. **The old world** — built for the human software lifecycle, and good at it. Code in, code kept, forever.
2. **The shift** — now agents and humans build together. Work happens that no human watches. The old world can store that work but can't *account* for it — a record with no memory.
3. **The migration** — you set out for the new world, one built for both kinds of builders. Your crew is already mixed: you, a ship AI, a bay of drones. (Nice touch: this is your first time really working *with* agents — the game is also your first day in the new era.)
4. **The fall** — a bad jump, the ship's memory faults, nothing to rebuild from. Planetfall. *Hey — that's the title earning its keep: the fall is what working without a record looks like.*
5. **The rebuild** — your three levels, exactly as built: bank your own work (L1), let agents work unwatched and read the record (L2), answer for all of it from the record alone (L3).
6. **The liftoff** — you don't limp back to the old world for repairs. You fly on, and the ship flies *because* every bolt of it is accounted for. You haven't just fixed the ship — you've already arrived, in the sense that matters: you work like the new world now.

What I'd change in the actual game is small, because your levels already tell the middle of this story perfectly:

- **An opening of 4–5 dialogue beats** (the Bug Bash pattern we discussed) delivering beats 1–4 — this finally gives the ship AI's amnesia a *cause* and the player a destination.
- **One word-level shift everywhere:** the current copy says restoring the ship can "take you home." Change home → onward. You're not going back. That's very Entire.
- **The liftoff ending** gets one line about flying on the record / on toward the new world, right above the `npx skills add` line that's already there.

The thing I'd deliberately leave vague: the new planet itself. Don't show it, don't name it, don't promise "everything just works" there — that's the unimplemented-features trap in fiction form. The destination can stay a direction rather than a place; the *way of working* is what the player actually takes with them.

Want me to draft the opening beats as actual copy — title-screen-into-crash, in the ship AI's voice — so you can react to real lines instead of an outline?

> AGENT

Honest answer: it was an instinct from our earlier conversation — one character, one box, one voice across the whole game — not a hard requirement. But your question made me actually test the idea, and there's a version of it that's much better than what I had in my head, and a real argument against it too. Let me give you both.

**The case for the AI's voice:** the opening would be the only time you ever hear the ship's AI *intact* — confident, complete, mid-migration, telling you why you left. Then the jump goes wrong and its memory faults mid-sentence — the last coherent thing it says. Cut to the island, Level 1, and the same voice is the amnesiac asking you who it is. The opening narrator and the thing you spend the game repairing are the same character, and you *heard* what was lost. That makes the amnesia a wound instead of a premise, and it makes L3 — where the restored AI reads its own record back to you — the completed arc: voice lost, voice rebuilt from checkpoints. It's the strongest emotional version, and it's cheap: it's just who the text is attributed to.

**The case against:** beats 1–2 (the old world, the shift to agents) aren't really the ship's story to tell — they're *yours*, the developer's. An AI narrating "the world was built for humans only" is slightly odd from the mouth of an agent. And there's a logic wrinkle: if the AI loses all memory, it narrating the pre-crash events to the *player* only works if you treat the opening as something the player witnessed, not a recording.

So the clean split, if you want the best of both: **beats 1–3 as plain title cards** (Bug Bash style — "Mona is working late..." voice, no speaker), covering the world, the shift, the departure — and then **beat 4 hands off to the ship AI** for the jump and the fault, so the last thing before planetfall is its voice degrading. Narrator sets the world; the AI's first appearance is the moment it breaks. You meet the character at the exact moment the game's premise happens to it.

That's the version I'd write. But if you'd rather keep it simpler — all title cards, no speaker at all, AI doesn't appear until L1 — that also works and is exactly what Bug Bash does. Which way do you want the draft?

Same beats, plainer language:

What changed: "the jump went wrong" → "on the way, your ship broke"; "shattered across a lavender sea" → "its memory was lost" (and "scattered" already exists in the L1 briefing, so the island copy still connects); "fly on" → "fly again"; "from the very first day" → "you love working this way."

One thing worth deciding while we're here: the existing briefings have the same issue in places — "the sky turns against you," "the clock has an opinion," "banked" itself is an idiom (poker/banking metaphor). Options: keep it but introduce it gently ("link a checkpoint to save it — we call this banking it"), or swap to "save" everywhere. Keeping "bank" with a one-time introduction is my lean, since "freeze keeps it, checkpoint banks it" is your best teaching line and rhythm matters there.
